title: Nonsurgical Therapy for Hydrocephalus: A Comprehensive and Critical Survey

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Biological Foundations of Hydrocephalus Relevant to Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.subsection_title: Definitions and clinical classifications of hydrocephalus
subsections.content:
Hydrocephalus is best understood as a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by disturbed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation, altered intracranial compliance, and secondary ventricular enlargement, rather than simply excess CSF volume. Modern definitions emphasize imbalance among CSF production, flow, and absorption within the ventricular–subarachnoid system and its interaction with brain parenchyma ref [1], ref [2]. This broader framing is important for nonsurgical therapy because ventricular size alone does not capture disease activity, pressure dynamics, or reversibility.

Clinically, hydrocephalus is commonly classified by presumed site and mechanism of CSF disturbance: noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus, in which intraventricular pathways are blocked; communicating hydrocephalus, in which ventricular pathways remain patent but CSF transfer or absorption is impaired; and forms associated with altered venous, pulsatile, or compliance-related physiology ref [2], ref [3]. Temporal and etiologic classifications are also widely used, including congenital versus acquired disease and posthemorrhagic, postinfectious, tumor-related, malformative, traumatic, and idiopathic forms ref [4], ref [5]. In pediatrics, these categories map onto distinct developmental vulnerabilities and prognostic trajectories.

A further major distinction is between pediatric hydrocephalus and adult chronic hydrocephalus syndromes, especially idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), which presents with gait, cognitive, and urinary symptoms despite often modest mean CSF pressure elevations ref [6], ref [7]. International and neurosurgical guidelines therefore recommend classification frameworks that integrate age, cause, anatomy, symptom complex, and expected response to CSF diversion rather than relying on a single binary scheme ref [5], ref [8]. Such multidimensional classification is particularly relevant when considering medical or supportive alternatives, because the plausibility of nonsurgical intervention depends on the underlying pathophysiological subtype ref [1], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Biological Foundations of Hydrocephalus Relevant to Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.content:
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) physiology is central to hydrocephalus because ventricular enlargement reflects not simply excess fluid volume, but disordered production, circulation, compliance, and clearance. Classical models emphasized choroid plexus secretion with unidirectional flow through the ventricles to arachnoid villous absorption, an architecture synthesized by Davson and Welch and later challenged by experimental work showing substantial exchange across capillary, ependymal, and interstitial compartments ref [9], ref [10]. Modern formulations therefore treat CSF as part of a coupled craniospinal fluid system linked to cerebral blood volume, brain viscoelasticity, and glymphatic-interstitial transport ref [11], ref [12].

Hydrodynamically, pulsatile arterial inflow and venous outflow generate cyclical CSF motion through the aqueduct and subarachnoid spaces, while intracranial compliance determines whether these oscillations are buffered or transmitted as pathological pressure gradients. The pressure-volume relationship described by Marmarou helps explain why small increments in intracranial volume can sharply raise pressure once compensatory reserve is exhausted ref [13]. Phase-contrast MRI studies further demonstrate altered aqueductal stroke volume and redistributed pulsatility in hydrocephalus, although these measures are physiologic markers rather than stand-alone diagnostic criteria ref [14], ref [15].

These concepts are especially relevant to nonsurgical intervention because they broaden therapeutic targets beyond bulk diversion. Disturbed CSF dynamics may arise from impaired absorption after hemorrhage or inflammation, altered venous compliance, ependymal and periventricular water transport, or sleep-dependent clearance dysfunction ref [11], ref [12], ref [16]. Experimental data also implicate aquaporin-4 in brain water handling and ventricular enlargement, reinforcing the view that hydrocephalus involves integrated fluid exchange across CSF, interstitial, vascular, and lymphatic pathways rather than a single obstructed conduit ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Biological Foundations of Hydrocephalus Relevant to Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.content:
Hydrocephalus arises from heterogeneous etiological pathways that disturb cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production, circulation, pulsatile transmission, or absorption. Classical obstruction remains a central mechanism, particularly aqueductal stenosis and outlet obstruction of the fourth ventricle, but contemporary models emphasize that "communicating" forms also reflect impaired CSF exchange across arachnoid granulations, ventricular and subarachnoid compliance abnormalities, and altered glymphatic-interstitial fluid transport rather than a simple absence of blockage ref [3], ref [12]. In posthemorrhagic and postinfectious hydrocephalus, blood products and inflammatory fibrosis can obstruct CSF pathways and impair resorptive surfaces, linking acute injury to chronic ventricular enlargement ref [18], ref [19].

Developmental hydrocephalus often reflects disrupted ependymal-ciliary biology and aberrant neurodevelopmental signaling. Experimental and human genetic studies implicate defects in motile cilia, planar cell polarity, and ependymal integrity, which compromise directional CSF flow and may also alter periventricular stem-cell niches ref [20], ref [21]. In addition, mutations in L1CAM define a well-established cause of X-linked hydrocephalus with aqueductal stenosis, illustrating how cell-adhesion and axon-guidance pathways can converge on ventricular outflow failure ref [22].

These initiating mechanisms drive downstream disease pathways that are relevant to nonsurgical therapy: periventricular edema, white-matter stretch and ischemia, neuroinflammation, gliosis, and altered cerebral blood flow. Work in normal pressure hydrocephalus further suggests that venous dysfunction and reduced intracranial compliance contribute to symptom generation even when gross obstruction is absent ref [23], ref [24]. Etiological stratification is therefore essential, because anti-inflammatory, antifibrotic, neuroprotective, or rehabilitation-based strategies are most plausible when matched to the dominant biological pathway rather than the radiographic phenotype alone.

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Biological Foundations of Hydrocephalus Relevant to Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.subsection_title: Neuropathological consequences of untreated or progressive hydrocephalus
subsections.content:
Untreated or progressive hydrocephalus produces a characteristic pattern of brain injury driven by chronic ventricular distension, altered pulsatility, and impaired perfusion. Experimental and clinicopathological studies indicate that the earliest structural damage often localizes to periventricular white matter, where stretch and ischemia disrupt axons, oligodendroglia, and myelin, with secondary gliosis and extracellular edema ref [25], ref [26]. These changes are not merely radiographic correlates of ventriculomegaly; they provide a plausible substrate for gait dysfunction, psychomotor slowing, and impaired attention across age groups.

With continued progression, injury extends beyond white matter to the ependymal lining, subependymal microenvironment, and cortex. Denudation of ependyma and altered periventricular homeostasis have been documented in hydrocephalic brain and may further impair cerebrospinal fluid-interstitial exchange ref [27]. In animal models, chronic hydrocephalus is associated with reduced cerebral blood flow, disturbed blood-brain barrier properties, neuroinflammation, and synaptic and dendritic abnormalities, supporting the view that hydrocephalus is a diffuse disorder of brain tissue rather than a purely mechanical enlargement of the ventricles ref [28], ref [29], ref [30].

Neuropathological burden also depends on developmental timing and duration. In the immature brain, ventricular enlargement can interfere with proliferation zones and white matter maturation, contributing to long-term cognitive and motor disability ref [31]. In older adults, chronic hydrocephalus overlaps with age-related and neurodegenerative pathologies; cortical biopsies and imaging-pathology studies have reported Alzheimer-type changes in some patients, complicating prognosis and limiting reversibility when treatment is delayed ref [32], ref [33]. These observations underscore the importance of early recognition when considering nonsurgical measures aimed at preserving function or slowing progression.

subsections.section_title: Clinical and Biological Foundations of Hydrocephalus Relevant to Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.content:
The natural history of hydrocephalus is highly age- and etiology-dependent, but a common theme is that prolonged ventricular enlargement and altered CSF pulsatility can convert potentially reversible dysfunction into established tissue injury. Experimental and clinical work indicates that early phases are characterized by impaired periventricular perfusion, transependymal fluid shift, and white-matter distortion before widespread neuronal loss becomes fixed, supporting the concept of a finite therapeutic window for interventions that aim to modify disease biology rather than only divert CSF ref [34], ref [35].

In infants and children, timing is especially critical because hydrocephalus unfolds during rapid brain growth. Classic neurodevelopmental studies showed that delayed control of posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation is associated with worse cognitive and motor outcomes, while animal models demonstrate progressive axonal injury, myelin disruption, and ischemic change with sustained ventriculomegaly ref [36], ref [37]. These observations imply that nonsurgical strategies would need either to prevent secondary injury early or to complement temporizing care while irreversible developmental consequences are still avoidable.

In adults, the concept of a therapeutic window is well illustrated by idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus, where gait and urinary symptoms often precede more entrenched cognitive decline, and shorter symptom duration predicts better postoperative recovery ref [38], ref [39]. Imaging and biomarker studies further suggest that increasing comorbid neurodegeneration narrows reversibility, complicating both prognosis and trial design ref [40], ref [41]. Across hydrocephalus phenotypes, therefore, the natural history argues for stage-specific intervention: early disease may be amenable to neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, or CSF-dynamic modulation, whereas late disease is dominated by established structural damage and reduced plasticity ref [35], ref [41].

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Biological Approaches to Nonsurgical Management
subsections.content:
Pharmacologic suppression of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production has historically centered on carbonic anhydrase inhibition and, to a lesser extent, loop diuretics. Acetazolamide reduces bicarbonate transport across the choroid plexus and thereby lowers CSF secretion, a mechanism established in classic experimental physiology and sustained by later translational work on epithelial ion transport in the plexus ref [42], ref [43]. In hydrocephalus, however, mechanistic plausibility has not translated into robust clinical benefit, particularly when structural CSF pathway obstruction or impaired absorption predominates over hypersecretion.

The main clinical experience comes from infant posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, where acetazolamide, usually combined with furosemide, was tested as a temporizing alternative to surgical diversion. Early observational reports suggested possible slowing of ventricular enlargement, but randomized evidence failed to confirm benefit and instead raised concern for harm. The multicenter trial by Kennedy et al. found no reduction in shunt surgery and identified more adverse events in treated infants ref [44]. A subsequent Cochrane review concluded that acetazolamide plus furosemide is neither effective nor safe for posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, with increased risks including metabolic derangement and nephrocalcinosis ref [45]. Related neonatal studies further documented frequent biochemical complications during therapy ref [46], ref [47].

Accordingly, agents targeting CSF production now occupy a limited role in contemporary management. Their failure likely reflects both modest achievable reductions in CSF formation and the multifactorial pathophysiology of hydrocephalus after hemorrhage or infection. Experimental interest persists in more selective modulation of choroid plexus transporters and channels, including Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransport mechanisms implicated in posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus pathogenesis ref [48], but these approaches remain preclinical rather than established therapy ref [49].

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Biological Approaches to Nonsurgical Management
subsections.content:
Osmotic and pressure-modulating therapies have been used primarily as temporizing measures to lower intracranial pressure rather than to correct the underlying disturbance in cerebrospinal fluid circulation. Hyperosmolar agents reduce brain water by creating an osmotic gradient across the blood-brain barrier, but their effectiveness depends on barrier integrity, serum osmolality, and hemodynamic status. In broader neurocritical care, mannitol has long been standard therapy for intracranial hypertension, although contemporary recommendations increasingly place hypertonic saline alongside or above mannitol because of more sustained intracranial pressure reduction and less diuresis-related hypotension ref [50], ref [51], ref [52].

Evidence specific to hydrocephalus is substantially weaker. Early experimental work suggested that osmotherapeutic agents can transiently decrease ventricular size or intracranial pressure, but these effects are short-lived and do not reliably restore CSF outflow. In children with acute hydrocephalus, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to support osmotic agents such as mannitol or glycerol as definitive treatment, emphasizing the lack of robust randomized data ref [53]. Acetazolamide-furosemide combinations, sometimes framed as pressure-lowering medical therapy, have likewise shown inconsistent benefit in posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation of prematurity and have not displaced surgical CSF diversion ref [54], ref [55].

Hypertonic saline has attracted interest because it may improve cerebral perfusion while lowering intracranial pressure, and consensus statements for pediatric severe traumatic brain injury support its use for intracranial hypertension ref [56], ref [57]. However, extrapolation to hydrocephalus should be cautious: repeated hyperosmolar therapy carries risks of electrolyte disturbance, renal injury, rebound intracranial hypertension, and masking of progressive ventricular enlargement. Accordingly, these therapies are best viewed as bridges in acute decompensation or perioperative stabilization rather than durable nonsurgical management of hydrocephalus ref [51], ref [52], ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Biological Approaches to Nonsurgical Management
subsections.content:
Anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective therapies have been pursued to attenuate the secondary injury cascade triggered by intraventricular and subarachnoid blood, including microglial activation, ependymal and periventricular damage, oxidative stress, and cytokine-driven disturbance of CSF circulation. Experimental work has repeatedly implicated transforming growth factor-β signaling and innate immune activation in posthemorrhagic ventricular enlargement, providing a mechanistic basis for pharmacologic intervention beyond simple pressure control ref [58], ref [59]. However, translation has been difficult because candidate agents must act within a narrow temporal window and are often tested in heterogeneous neonatal or adult hemorrhagic hydrocephalus phenotypes.

Historical anti-inflammatory approaches have produced mixed or negative clinical results. In premature infants with posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, the multicenter dexamethasone trial by Whitelaw and colleagues did not show clear benefit and raised concern regarding adverse effects, limiting enthusiasm for corticosteroids as routine therapy ref [60]. By contrast, ibuprofen reduced prostaglandin-mediated CSF secretion in experimental settings and modestly altered ventricular expansion in neonatal models, but convincing human efficacy data remain lacking ref [61]. Broader neuroprotective strategies such as erythropoietin are biologically attractive because they combine anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory effects; nevertheless, evidence in hemorrhage-associated hydrocephalus remains preclinical and indirect despite encouraging neonatal brain-injury literature ref [62].

More targeted approaches are now centered on iron toxicity, complement, and inflammatory signaling. Iron chelation with deferoxamine attenuated ventricular enlargement, white-matter injury, and inflammation after intraventricular hemorrhage in animal models ref [63], while minocycline has shown suppression of microglial activation and tissue injury in related hemorrhagic brain-injury paradigms ref [64]. Experimental blockade of Toll-like receptor 4 and downstream NF-κB pathways has also reduced posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus severity in rodents ref [65], and complement activation has emerged as another plausible therapeutic axis ref [66]. Overall, anti-inflammatory/neuroprotective therapy remains mechanistically compelling but insufficiently validated clinically, with major gaps in dosing, developmental safety, and patient selection.

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Biological Approaches to Nonsurgical Management
subsections.content:
Fibrinolytic and hemorrhage-directed therapies are intended to accelerate clearance of intraventricular or subarachnoid blood, thereby limiting obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid pathways, dampening inflammatory scarring, and potentially reducing shunt dependence. The strongest clinical experience comes from intraventricular thrombolysis for intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). Early randomized data suggested that low-dose recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) hastens ventricular clot resolution without a clear excess of rebleeding, although improvement in functional outcome remained uncertain ref [67], ref [68]. The phase III CLEAR III trial confirmed more rapid clot removal with alteplase through an external ventricular drain but did not show a statistically significant improvement in the primary functional endpoint, despite signals for reduced mortality and possible benefit with greater clot evacuation ref [69].

Mechanistically, these interventions target one of the key drivers of post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus: persistent blood products within the ventricular system and basal cisterns. Experimental and translational work has linked hemoglobin, iron, and transforming growth factor-beta signaling to arachnoid fibrosis and impaired CSF absorption, providing a rationale for early blood clearance and adjunctive iron-directed strategies ref [70], ref [71]. In premature infants with posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, direct fibrinolytic approaches have been explored, but enthusiasm has been tempered by safety concerns and inconsistent neurodevelopmental benefit; notably, DRIFT (drainage, irrigation and fibrinolytic therapy) improved some long-term cognitive outcomes in follow-up despite procedural complexity and early adverse events ref [72], ref [73].

Outside intraventricular thrombolysis, systemic hemorrhage-directed approaches such as tranexamic acid are relevant chiefly to preventing hematoma expansion rather than treating established CSF pathway obstruction. Large trials in spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage have shown modest effects on early bleeding dynamics without convincing functional benefit, limiting their role in hydrocephalus prevention ref [74]. Overall, fibrinolytic treatment remains biologically plausible and technically attractive in selected hemorrhagic hydrocephalus phenotypes, but current evidence supports a nuanced view: radiographic clot clearance is reproducibly improved, whereas durable patient-centered benefit is less consistent and highly dependent on timing, clot burden, and age-specific risk profiles ref [69], ref [72], ref [75].

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Biological Approaches to Nonsurgical Management
subsections.content:
Experimental molecular and targeted therapies aim to move beyond nonspecific pressure reduction by intervening in pathways that govern cerebrospinal fluid secretion, ventricular fibrosis, and secondary parenchymal injury. A major mechanistic focus has been the choroid plexus, where the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter NKCC1 and related ion-transport machinery contribute to CSF production; developmental and injury-state changes in this epithelium suggest a plausible target for pharmacologic modulation ref [76], ref [77]. Similarly, aquaporin biology has been investigated because AQP1 is enriched in the choroid plexus and AQP4 in periventricular astroglia, linking water transport to ventricular enlargement and edema propagation ref [78], ref [79].

Posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus has also prompted targeted anti-fibrotic and signaling-based approaches. Transforming growth factor-beta signaling is strongly implicated in arachnoid and ependymal scarring after intraventricular blood exposure, and experimental blockade of this axis reduces extracellular matrix deposition and hydrocephalus severity in preclinical models ref [80], ref [81]. Parallel work has examined iron-mediated toxicity and inflammatory patterning after hemorrhage, with iron chelation by deferoxamine attenuating ventricular dilation and tissue injury in animal studies ref [82]. Other pathway-directed strategies include antagonism of toll-like receptor 4 or downstream inflammatory cascades, motivated by evidence that hemoglobin breakdown products drive innate immune activation and CSF flow obstruction after hemorrhage ref [83].

Despite strong mechanistic rationale, translation remains limited. Most candidate therapies are supported predominantly by neonatal or rodent models, while target expression, blood-CSF barrier penetration, and therapeutic windows vary substantially across age groups and hydrocephalus etiologies ref [76], ref [79], ref [83]. Accordingly, these approaches are best viewed as hypothesis-driven adjuncts whose eventual clinical value will depend on biomarker-guided patient selection, compartment-specific pharmacokinetics, and demonstration that pathway modulation meaningfully alters shunt dependence or neurodevelopmental outcome.

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Biological Approaches to Nonsurgical Management
subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacokinetics, dosing challenges, and age-specific considerations
subsections.content:
Pharmacological management of hydrocephalus and related intracranial pressure disorders is constrained by highly variable CNS exposure, short therapeutic windows, and immature elimination pathways in infants. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and loop diuretics exemplify this problem: although acetazolamide can reduce cerebrospinal fluid secretion experimentally, neonatal and infant dosing is limited by metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbance, and unpredictable penetration into CSF and brain, while furosemide adds risks of natriuresis, ototoxicity, and nephrocalcinosis without clear durable efficacy in posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation ref [84], ref [85], ref [86]. Historical trials of acetazolamide plus furosemide in preterm infants ultimately underscored that plausible mechanism does not compensate for poor therapeutic index in a population with rapidly changing renal handling and acid-base reserve ref [54].

Osmotic agents pose parallel pharmacokinetic challenges. Mannitol requires an intact osmotic gradient and adequate renal clearance; repeated dosing may accumulate in brain tissue or produce rebound intracranial hypertension, especially when blood-brain barrier integrity is impaired ref [87]. Hypertonic saline offers more predictable intravascular expansion, but optimal concentration, infusion strategy, and sodium targets remain age- and disease-specific, with pediatric TBI guidance emphasizing careful monitoring of serum sodium, osmolality, hemodynamics, and renal function rather than fixed adult-derived regimens ref [88], ref [57].

Age-specific considerations are therefore central. Preterm neonates have low glomerular filtration, reduced protein binding, distinct total body water compartments, and ongoing blood-brain barrier maturation, all of which alter volume of distribution and clearance. Intraventricular or systemic hemorrhage may further distort CSF turnover and ventricular drug distribution. Contemporary pediatric formularies and neonatal pharmacology reviews consistently recommend weight-based dosing, developmental adjustment, and close laboratory surveillance, while recognizing that robust PK/PD data for many agents used in hydrocephalus are still lacking ref [89], ref [90].

subsections.section_title: Supportive, Rehabilitative, and Nonoperative Symptom-Oriented Care
subsections.content:
Medical stabilization in chronic hydrocephalus or shunt-dependent states is primarily supportive and aims to prevent secondary injury while clarifying whether definitive CSF diversion can be deferred. In adults with suspected normal-pressure hydrocephalus, conservative management includes systematic review of comorbid gait, cognitive, and urinary contributors, optimization of vascular risk factors, and repeated clinical reassessment because symptom evolution and response to prognostic testing are heterogeneous [1,2]. When surgery is not immediately feasible, careful medication reconciliation is also important to avoid drug-induced worsening of cognition, postural instability, or bladder symptoms that can confound assessment.

In infants and children, temporary conservative strategies may be used only in selected circumstances and usually serve as bridges rather than durable therapy. Serial lumbar puncture or ventricular taps have historically been used in posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, but randomized evidence does not support repeated tapping as a routine means of improving major outcomes [3]. Temporizing devices such as ventricular access reservoirs or ventriculosubgaleal shunts may stabilize progressive ventricular enlargement until the infant is large enough for definitive treatment [4,5]. Acetazolamide with furosemide was once explored to reduce CSF production, but a multicenter trial found no benefit and potential harm, so it is not recommended as standard conservative therapy [6].

Across age groups, conservative management also includes surveillance for raised intracranial pressure, hydration and electrolyte management, treatment of constipation and urinary dysfunction, skin care in immobilized patients, and prompt recognition of shunt malfunction or infection in previously treated individuals. Consensus statements on idiopathic intracranial hypertension further illustrate the broader principle that weight management, headache control, and visual monitoring can be central elements of nonsurgical stabilization when operative intervention is deferred [7,8]. In previously shunted hydrocephalus, structured follow-up remains essential because late shunt failure is common and clinical deterioration may be subtle [9].

subsections.section_title: Supportive, Rehabilitative, and Nonoperative Symptom-Oriented Care
subsections.content:
In infants and children managed nonoperatively or while awaiting definitive treatment, supportive care should be framed around neurodevelopmental surveillance rather than symptom control alone. Early standardized assessment of cognition, language, motor skills, and adaptive behavior is important because children with chronic neurosurgical or neurologic conditions often show deficits that evolve over time rather than remaining static. Broad pediatric rehabilitation principles support longitudinal developmental monitoring and early intervention to reduce secondary disability and optimize participation in home and school settings ref [100], ref [101].

For medically complex infants, especially those with hydrocephalus or brain injury, developmental care in the NICU and early infancy can influence later outcomes. Family-centered developmental programs such as NIDCAP have been associated with improved neurobehavioral organization and later developmental performance in preterm populations, supporting the use of structured environmental modification, caregiver coaching, and cue-based handling in vulnerable children ref [102], ref [103]. In parallel, early intervention services grounded in developmental and task-specific therapy can improve cognitive and motor outcomes in high-risk infants and should be integrated promptly when delays emerge ref [104], ref [105].

School-aged children benefit from coordinated educational planning, physical and occupational therapy, speech-language therapy, and psychosocial support. Pediatric rehabilitation frameworks emphasize goal-directed, participation-focused care and routine reassessment as children encounter new developmental demands ref [101], ref [106]. Caregiver mental health and family functioning also warrant attention, as parent-mediated and family-centered programs can improve child participation and reduce stress in chronic neurodevelopmental disability ref [107].

Where symptoms remain stable enough to permit observation, supportive follow-up should include serial developmental screening, hearing and vision assessment when relevant, and anticipatory guidance for transition across infancy, school entry, and adolescence. Such monitoring is particularly important because early developmental trajectories can predict later functional independence and quality of life ref [105], ref [106], ref [108].

subsections.section_title: Supportive, Rehabilitative, and Nonoperative Symptom-Oriented Care
subsections.content:
Cognitive, gait, and functional rehabilitation are central components of nonoperative care for patients with chronic ventriculomegaly or hydrocephalus-related disability, particularly when symptoms evolve gradually or surgery is deferred. In adults, multidomain impairment often spans gait, executive function, balance, continence-related self-management, and activities of daily living; accordingly, rehabilitation is typically interdisciplinary and goal directed rather than disease specific. Observational studies in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus have shown that gait dysfunction is often the most measurable deficit and can be quantified with timed walking tests, dual-task paradigms, and balance assessment, while cognition and function may require parallel neuropsychological and occupational therapy evaluation ref [109], ref [110].

Task-specific gait training, balance therapy, lower-extremity strengthening, cueing strategies, and fall-prevention education are reasonable supportive measures to preserve mobility and reduce secondary deconditioning. The broader neurorehabilitation literature supports aerobic and progressive exercise for improving walking capacity and physical function in neurological populations ref [111], ref [112], and small hydrocephalus-focused studies suggest that structured physical activity may be feasible and beneficial after diagnosis or shunting, especially when combined with standardized outcome assessment ref [113], ref [114]. Occupational therapy can address transfers, dressing, toileting, home safety, and caregiver instruction, while cognitive rehabilitation may target attention, processing speed, and compensatory strategies for executive dysfunction, domains commonly impaired in normal pressure hydrocephalus ref [110], ref [115].

Importantly, rehabilitation should not be viewed solely as adjunctive to surgery. In frail patients, it may help maintain function while candidacy is clarified, and in those with partial or no surgical response it remains essential for long-term disability management. Serial functional measures such as the Timed Up and Go, 10-m walk, Berg Balance Scale, Functional Independence Measure, and disease-specific gait scales can provide clinically meaningful monitoring of rehabilitation response ref [109], ref [114], ref [116].

subsections.section_title: Supportive, Rehabilitative, and Nonoperative Symptom-Oriented Care
subsections.subsection_title: Management of symptoms and quality of life
subsections.content:
Symptom-oriented management is central for patients managed nonoperatively or while awaiting surgery, because headache, gait limitation, pain, sleep disturbance, bladder dysfunction, and cognitive or affective symptoms often drive disability more than imaging alone. In adults with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, gait and balance impairment are major determinants of falls and loss of independence, while urinary and cognitive symptoms substantially affect caregiver burden and health-related quality of life; structured assessment with disease-specific and generic patient-reported outcome measures can therefore guide supportive interventions and realistic counseling ref [117], ref [118], ref [119].

Rehabilitative symptom management should be individualized and multidisciplinary. Targeted balance and gait training, cueing strategies, assistive devices, home-safety modification, continence support, and treatment of comorbid sleep and mood disorders are reasonable adjuncts, particularly when surgery is deferred or expected to yield only partial recovery. Evidence from post-shunt rehabilitation studies suggests that supervised exercise can improve functional performance beyond surgery alone, supporting a broader role for physical therapy even in conservatively managed patients ref [113]. In parallel, cognitive rehabilitation, caregiver education, and social support are important because executive dysfunction and apathy commonly persist and correlate with reduced participation ref [119], ref [120].

For children and young adults with chronic hydrocephalus, quality-of-life management also extends beyond ventricular control. Long-term outcome studies show persistent challenges in school participation, fatigue, motor performance, psychosocial adjustment, and family stress despite survival into adulthood ref [121], ref [122]. Accordingly, symptom management should include neuropsychological follow-up, educational accommodations, management of headache and visual symptoms, and anticipatory support during developmental transitions. Standardized health-related quality-of-life instruments developed for hydrocephalus can help capture these broader treatment goals and complement neurological examination and imaging during longitudinal care ref [123].

subsections.section_title: Supportive, Rehabilitative, and Nonoperative Symptom-Oriented Care
subsections.content:
For patients managed expectantly, monitoring aims to detect radiographic progression, emerging myelopathy, and decline in gait, continence, cognition, or cranial-nerve function before irreversible disability develops. In hydrocephalus and other CSF-disorder populations, serial clinical review should be paired with interval neuroimaging, because ventricular size alone may correlate imperfectly with symptom burden and treatment need ref [7], ref [124]. In suspected normal-pressure hydrocephalus, longitudinal assessment is especially important when surgery is deferred, with repeated documentation of gait, cognition, and urinary symptoms and selective use of prognostic tests such as large-volume lumbar tap or external lumbar drainage when candidacy is reconsidered ref [125], ref [126].

Imaging surveillance should be tailored to the underlying lesion and tempo of disease. For incidental or minimally symptomatic meningioma, several series support active monitoring with MRI because many tumors grow slowly, although a subset shows clinically meaningful progression that justifies risk-stratified follow-up rather than uniformly prolonged intervals ref [127], ref [128]. In vestibular schwannoma, observation with serial MRI and audiovestibular testing is also well established, particularly for small tumors and older or medically frail patients, but growth and hearing decline remain common enough to require predefined triggers for intervention ref [129]. Similar principles apply to selected low-grade gliomas, where carefully structured surveillance can be appropriate in highly selected cases, provided imaging and neurological review remain rigorous ref [130].

Across diagnoses, best practice is not passive delay but protocolized follow-up: standardized neurological examination, patient-reported symptom tracking, objective functional measures, and comparison of sequential imaging using the same modality and planes. Surveillance plans should also account for age-specific risks, since pediatric conditions such as asymptomatic ventriculomegaly or Chiari-related CSF abnormalities may evolve with development and require reevaluation over time ref [131].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Appraisal Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.content:
In congenital and neonatal hydrocephalus, evidence for nonsurgical therapy remains limited and largely adjunctive rather than definitive. Historical attempts to suppress cerebrospinal fluid production with acetazolamide, often combined with furosemide, were driven by physiologic plausibility but have not translated into reliable clinical benefit. The most influential neonatal data come from trials in posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation showing no meaningful reduction in shunt dependence and signals of harm, including increased neurologic morbidity, which has strongly tempered enthusiasm for applying the same strategy to broader neonatal hydrocephalus populations ref [55], ref [45]. Earlier pharmacologic reports in infants with hydrocephalus were small and uncontrolled, and did not establish durable efficacy ref [132], ref [133].

For congenital hydrocephalus specifically, heterogeneity in etiology is a major reason medical therapy has underperformed. Malformative causes such as aqueductal stenosis, posterior fossa crowding, or complex genetic/developmental brain anomalies involve persistent obstruction or altered brain compliance that are unlikely to respond to diuretics alone. Contemporary reviews of neonatal hydrocephalus management therefore continue to regard temporizing drainage or definitive CSF diversion as the standard of care, with medication playing at most a short-term supportive role when surgery must be delayed ref [134], ref [4]. This caution is reinforced by broader analyses of infant hydrocephalus outcomes emphasizing that early control of ventricular expansion, rather than prolonged pharmacologic trials, is the key determinant of neurodevelopmental protection ref [135].

Accordingly, in congenital and neonatal hydrocephalus, nonsurgical treatment should be appraised as low-certainty and context-specific. It may be considered only in medically unstable infants, in resource-limited bridging scenarios, or as part of individualized palliative care, but not as a proven substitute for neurosurgical management. Recent overviews of pediatric hydrocephalus and global neurosurgical practice similarly conclude that there is no established disease-modifying medical therapy for congenital neonatal hydrocephalus at present ref [35], ref [136].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Appraisal Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.content:
Posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus of prematurity (PHH) is the setting in which nonsurgical therapy has been most rigorously tested, and the overall signal is largely negative. Pharmacologic suppression of cerebrospinal fluid production with acetazolamide plus furosemide did not reduce the need for shunt placement and was associated with increased adverse outcomes in randomized evidence, arguing against routine use of diuretic therapy in preterm infants with progressive ventricular dilatation ref [45]. Earlier fibrinolytic strategies were also disappointing: intraventricular streptokinase failed to improve shunt-free survival or major developmental outcomes in a multicenter trial ref [137].

Management has therefore shifted toward temporizing drainage and earlier monitoring-based intervention rather than medical therapy. Observational and trial data indicate that low-threshold treatment of progressive ventricular enlargement, guided by cranial ultrasonography rather than waiting for overt clinical signs, is associated with less brain injury and more favorable developmental profiles ref [138], ref [139]. The ELVIS randomized trial comparing low versus higher intervention thresholds did not show a large difference in the primary endpoint, but supported the safety and plausibility of earlier intervention, with subsequent analyses linking reduced ventricular distension to better neurodevelopment ref [140], ref [141].

Among adjunctive approaches, drainage, irrigation, and fibrinolytic therapy (DRIFT) provides the strongest evidence that modifying intraventricular blood burden may improve longer-term cognition despite substantial procedural complexity. In a randomized trial, DRIFT did not clearly reduce shunt surgery initially, but 2-year and 10-year follow-up demonstrated better cognitive outcomes than standard treatment ref [142], ref [143], ref [144]. Taken together, current evidence does not support diuretic or simple fibrinolytic drug therapy for PHH; benefit appears more likely from timely, image-guided CSF diversion and, in specialized centers, blood-clearing strategies aimed at limiting secondary white-matter injury.

subsections.section_title: Evidence Appraisal Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.content:
Infectious and inflammatory hydrocephalus is biologically distinct from other forms because CSF pathway obstruction, impaired arachnoid resorption, and ependymal injury are driven by active infection and host inflammatory cascades. The strongest nonsurgical data come from tuberculous meningitis (TBM), in which adjunctive corticosteroids improve survival overall and likely mitigate inflammation-related CSF outflow failure, although hydrocephalus-specific reversal is inconsistently reported ref [145], ref [146]. Aspirin has also been studied in TBM as host-directed therapy to reduce infarction and inflammatory vasculopathy, with randomized data suggesting potential benefit in selected patients, but evidence remains insufficient to recommend it specifically for hydrocephalus control ref [147], ref [148].

By contrast, medical treatment alone rarely provides definitive control when hydrocephalus accompanies pyogenic meningitis, ventriculitis, or fungal infection; prompt pathogen-directed antimicrobial therapy is necessary, but persistent ventricular enlargement often reflects organizing debris, loculation, or chronic arachnoid scarring rather than ongoing infection ref [149], ref [150]. In cryptococcal meningitis, however, serial therapeutic lumbar punctures represent an important nonsurgical strategy for raised intracranial pressure and can reduce mortality, even though they do not address established obstructive hydrocephalus in all cases ref [151], ref [152].

Overall, the evidence supports a context-specific approach: anti-inflammatory adjuncts are most defensible in TBM, pressure-lowering CSF drainage is central in cryptococcosis, and in bacterial or parasitic inflammatory hydrocephalus medical therapy is usually supportive or temporizing rather than curative. This heterogeneity helps explain why recommendations remain etiology-specific and why many patients ultimately require neurosurgical diversion despite appropriate anti-infective treatment ref [146], ref [150], ref [153].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Appraisal Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.content:
Evidence for nonsurgical therapy in tumor-related and other obstructive hydrocephalus is limited and largely adjunctive. In children with posterior fossa tumors, corticosteroids can transiently reduce peritumoral edema and may modestly improve cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pathway obstruction before definitive tumor resection, but they do not reliably control hydrocephalus itself. Acetazolamide and furosemide have historically been used to decrease CSF production, yet supportive data in obstructive hydrocephalus are sparse and inconsistent, with most experience extrapolated from pediatric hydrocephalus cohorts rather than tumor-specific trials ref [84], ref [154], ref [54].

The strongest modern evidence in this setting concerns perioperative temporization rather than durable medical control. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy has reduced reliance on pre-resection shunting for selected posterior fossa and tectal lesions, underscoring that the dominant mechanism is mechanical obstruction rather than a pharmacologically reversible disturbance of CSF physiology ref [155], ref [156]. In diffuse low-grade tectal glioma and other slowly progressive aqueductal lesions, observation with symptom-directed measures may be feasible, but sustained nonoperative treatment of hydrocephalus remains uncommon because progression can be abrupt and vision or consciousness may deteriorate ref [157], ref [158].

Accordingly, medical therapy is best framed as a bridge in patients awaiting surgery, receiving palliative oncologic care, or deemed temporarily unfit for intervention. Osmotic agents and corticosteroids may provide short-lived relief when intracranial pressure is driven partly by tumor-associated edema, but persistent ventricular enlargement generally requires CSF diversion or lesion-directed treatment. This pattern is reflected in contemporary hydrocephalus guidance, which does not support medications as definitive therapy for obstructive hydrocephalus except in highly selected or end-of-life contexts ref [35], ref [159].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Appraisal Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.content:
For idiopathic/normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), the evidence base for nonsurgical therapy is notably weak compared with shunt surgery. Consensus diagnostic work has emphasized that iNPH is a potentially treatable syndrome of gait, cognitive, and urinary dysfunction, but these guidelines do not identify any established disease-modifying medical therapy ref [91], ref [7]. Reviews of adult hydrocephalus similarly conclude that conservative management is largely supportive and directed at comorbidity control, rehabilitation, and careful patient selection rather than ventricular pathophysiology itself ref [8].

Pharmacologic efforts have focused mainly on agents intended to reduce CSF production or transiently alter fluid dynamics, especially acetazolamide. Small observational imaging studies suggested that low-dose acetazolamide may reduce periventricular hyperintensity and occasionally improve gait in selected patients, but these reports were uncontrolled and insufficient to define durable clinical benefit ref [160]. Earlier radionuclide cisternography-era experiences and isolated case reports also explored acetazolamide responsiveness, yet these approaches never matured into robust therapeutic evidence and have not displaced shunting as standard care ref [161], ref [162].

Accordingly, in iNPH the practical role of nonsurgical treatment is limited to temporizing care in poor operative candidates, optimization of vascular and neurodegenerative comorbidities, fall prevention, bladder symptom management, and physical therapy. This conservative stance is reinforced by prospective shunt studies showing substantially greater symptomatic improvement after surgery than would be expected from observation alone ref [163], ref [164]. Recent international guidance continues to frame pharmacologic therapy as unproven and supportive rather than definitive in iNPH ref [7], ref [165].

subsections.section_title: Evidence Appraisal Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.subsection_title: Hydrocephalus in medically fragile or nonsurgical candidates
subsections.content:
In medically fragile patients or those deemed poor operative candidates, nonsurgical hydrocephalus management is generally palliative, temporizing, or selectively adjunctive rather than definitively curative. Historical experience with carbonic anhydrase inhibition and diuretic therapy showed that acetazolamide, alone or combined with furosemide, can reduce cerebrospinal fluid production transiently, but durable control of ventricular enlargement or avoidance of shunting has not been consistently demonstrated ref [84], ref [166]. In neonatal and infant populations, randomized evidence failed to support routine acetazolamide–furosemide therapy and raised concern for excess adverse outcomes, limiting extrapolation to other frail groups ref [167].

For adults who cannot undergo shunt surgery because of severe comorbidity, anticoagulation, advanced malignancy, or limited life expectancy, evidence for medical therapy remains sparse. In idiopathic/normal-pressure hydrocephalus, small observational studies suggested short-term symptomatic improvement with low-dose acetazolamide in selected patients, with accompanying imaging changes in some cases, but these data are preliminary and not a substitute for CSF diversion ref [160], ref [168]. Serial lumbar puncture or temporary lumbar drainage may offer diagnostic clarification and brief symptom relief in selected communicating hydrocephalus, yet these approaches are burdensome and rarely durable as standalone treatment ref [92], ref [169].

Accordingly, treatment decisions in nonsurgical candidates should emphasize goals of care, reversibility of the underlying cause, and expected time horizon. Medical options may be reasonable as bridges, comfort-focused measures, or highly individualized trials when surgery is contraindicated, but current evidence does not support them as equivalent alternatives to definitive diversion in progressive hydrocephalus ref [166], ref [167], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Critical Evaluation of Limitations, Controversies, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Historical evolution of nonsurgical treatment paradigms
subsections.content:
The history of nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy is marked by repeated shifts between mechanistic optimism and clinical disappointment. Before shunting became dominant, medical approaches were largely empirical, aiming to reduce cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) production or intracranial pressure with osmotic agents and carbonic anhydrase inhibition. Experimental work showing that acetazolamide could decrease CSF formation helped establish the pharmacologic rationale for conservative treatment ref [170], while broader physiologic studies of CSF secretion and absorption reinforced the idea that hydrocephalus might be medically modifiable rather than purely surgical ref [171].

In practice, however, the modern era of drug therapy was defined less by durable disease modification than by attempts to postpone surgery, especially in infants with posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation. Randomized and multicenter studies of acetazolamide combined with furosemide failed to show benefit and raised safety concerns, helping to reverse earlier enthusiasm ref [54], ref [172]. Parallel experiences with repeated lumbar puncture or temporizing drainage similarly demonstrated that short-term control of ventricular size did not reliably translate into improved neurodevelopmental outcomes ref [173], ref [174]. These results shifted the field away from viewing nonsurgical therapy as a definitive alternative to CSF diversion.

More recent paradigms have broadened from simple CSF suppression toward mechanism-based neuroprotection, anti-fibrotic or anti-inflammatory strategies, and disease-specific management. Yet translational reviews emphasize that many candidate therapies succeed in animal models while failing in clinically heterogeneous human hydrocephalus, where timing, etiology, and irreversible white-matter injury constrain efficacy ref [84], ref [35]. The contemporary historical lesson is therefore not that nonsurgical treatment lacks biologic plausibility, but that prior paradigms often overgeneralized from CSF physiology to a complex syndrome requiring etiologically stratified intervention ref [1].

subsections.section_title: Critical Evaluation of Limitations, Controversies, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Quality and hierarchy of available evidence
subsections.content:
The evidentiary base for nonsurgical therapy in hydrocephalus sits low in the clinical hierarchy. Much of the literature consists of mechanistic animal studies or small, single-center clinical series, with few adequately powered randomized trials and limited replication across settings. This imbalance is visible in pharmacologic approaches such as acetazolamide and furosemide, where early physiological rationale and observational enthusiasm were not matched by durable clinical benefit in rigorous testing ref [84], ref [54]. Even when randomized evidence exists, as in posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation of prematurity, interventions have often targeted surrogate endpoints such as ventricular size or temporizing need rather than long-term neurodevelopmental function ref [175], ref [138].

A recurring problem is the mixture of distinct hydrocephalus entities within the same evidentiary conversation. Neonatal posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, congenital hydrocephalus, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and hydrocephalus secondary to infection or tumor differ in pathogenesis, natural history, and therapeutic window, yet studies often extrapolate across them. Systematic reviews and pediatric management guidelines repeatedly note that available studies are heterogeneous in entry criteria, co-interventions, and outcome definitions, limiting meta-analytic synthesis and external validity ref [176], ref [5].

Translational failures further expose weaknesses in the hierarchy of evidence. Promising preclinical anti-fibrotic or anti-inflammatory strategies, including transforming growth factor-beta pathway modulation, have strong mechanistic support in experimental hydrocephalus but remain sparsely tested in humans and without phase III confirmation ref [177], ref [178]. By contrast, the clearest high-level evidence in this field often derives from trials showing what does not work; the International PHVD Drug Trial found that acetazolamide plus furosemide was ineffective and potentially harmful, underscoring the need for multicenter, patient-centered trials before nonsurgical therapies can claim routine clinical utility ref [54], ref [167].

subsections.section_title: Critical Evaluation of Limitations, Controversies, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.content:
Outcome measurement is a central reason why nonsurgical hydrocephalus studies are difficult to compare and often fail to generate actionable evidence. Trials have used highly heterogeneous endpoints—ventricular size, intracranial pressure, head circumference, shunt avoidance, neurodevelopment, gait, cognition, or composite “clinical improvement” scores—despite weak correlations among these domains. In infant hydrocephalus, ventricular enlargement on imaging may not track functional recovery, while in adult syndromes such as idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), radiographic change can be modest even when symptoms improve ref [7], ref [91].

The problem is compounded by imperfect measurement tools. Classical imaging metrics such as the Evans index are convenient but coarse and were never intended as sensitive longitudinal biomarkers ref [179]. Clinical scales also have limitations: the iNPH grading scale improves standardization but remains partly subjective and vulnerable to inter-rater variability, comorbidity, and short-term fluctuation ref [180]. More detailed instruments, including structured gait assessments and neuropsychological batteries, are informative but resource-intensive and inconsistently implemented across centers ref [118], ref [181]. In pediatric studies, developmental outcomes are especially challenging because age-dependent trajectories, visual impairment, epilepsy, infection, and social determinants confound attribution of change to the hydrocephalus treatment itself ref [182].

These measurement issues create major risks of bias. Short follow-up may capture transient physiological effects without demonstrating durable functional benefit, whereas longer-term outcomes are often obscured by crossover to surgery and evolving disease biology. Consensus efforts have therefore emphasized multidimensional assessment, combining imaging, standardized clinical testing, patient-centered function, and complication reporting rather than relying on a single surrogate endpoint ref [91], ref [183]. For nonsurgical therapies, the absence of validated surrogate markers remains a major barrier to both early-phase screening and definitive efficacy trials ref [7], ref [183].

subsections.section_title: Critical Evaluation of Limitations, Controversies, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.content:
A central reason nonsurgical therapy remains difficult to evaluate is that “hydrocephalus” aggregates biologically distinct disorders. Neonatal posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, congenital aqueductal stenosis, tumor-related obstructive hydrocephalus, idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), and hydrocephalus associated with infection or neural tube defects differ in CSF dynamics, white-matter vulnerability, inflammatory burden, and therapeutic windows. Pediatric classifications have long emphasized this etiologic diversity, yet many interventional studies still pool patients across mechanisms, making signal dilution likely and limiting external validity ref [1], ref [2].

This heterogeneity is especially important for agents targeting specific pathophysiology. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition and osmotic strategies may be more plausible in states of excess CSF production or temporary pressure control, but are unlikely to reverse established ependymal disruption, gliosis, or arachnoid scarring. In posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus of prematurity, blood-product toxicity and inflammation appear central, whereas in iNPH the clinical phenotype overlaps with neurodegenerative and vascular disease, complicating prediction of response to any medical therapy ref [3], ref [4], ref [5]. The variable natural history of ventricular enlargement after intraventricular hemorrhage further illustrates why treatment timing and baseline risk must be incorporated into stratification rather than treated as nuisance variables ref [6].

Recent work points toward more refined stratification using imaging, physiology, and molecular markers. International and guideline-based efforts in iNPH stress that clinical diagnosis, radiographic pattern, and supplementary tests such as CSF tap testing identify subgroups with differing probabilities of reversibility, although these tools were developed mainly for shunt selection rather than drug trials ref [7], ref [8]. More broadly, phase-contrast MRI and related quantitative approaches demonstrate that CSF flow phenotypes are not uniform even within the same diagnostic label, supporting enrichment designs for future studies ref [9]. Without mechanism-based subgrouping, negative nonsurgical trials may continue to reflect cohort mixing more than true therapeutic inefficacy.

subsections.section_title: Critical Evaluation of Limitations, Controversies, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Safety, adverse effects, and ethical considerations
subsections.content:
Safety concerns have been a central reason why pharmacologic or other nonsurgical approaches have not displaced CSF diversion. Agents intended to reduce CSF production or modify intracranial dynamics often carry systemic toxicities that are difficult to justify in infants or neurologically vulnerable patients. Acetazolamide and furosemide can produce metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbance, nephrocalcinosis, dehydration, and poor weight gain, while the randomized evidence in posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation found no clinical benefit and possible harm, undermining risk-benefit justification ref [1], ref [2]. Similar concerns extend to osmotic agents and repeated lumbar puncture strategies, whose transient physiologic effects have not translated into durable outcome gains ref [3], ref [4].

Ethical difficulties are amplified by the epidemiology of hydrocephalus, because many candidate patients are premature neonates, infants, or cognitively impaired adults with limited decisional capacity. Trials therefore depend on surrogate consent, yet outcomes that matter to families long term may not align with short-term ventricular measurements or temporizing avoidance of shunt surgery. The landmark International Infant Hydrocephalus Study illustrated that even technically distinct treatments must ultimately be judged against neurodevelopmental outcome and treatment burden, not procedural ideology alone ref [5]. In normal-pressure hydrocephalus, the stakes differ but parallel concerns remain: delayed effective treatment may worsen reversibility, whereas exposing frail older adults to inadequately validated medical alternatives risks therapeutic misconception ref [6].

These issues are especially important in low-resource settings, where enthusiasm for low-cost nonsurgical options may reflect constrained access to surgery rather than strong efficacy data. Experience from Uganda showed that context-sensitive innovation can reduce dependence on shunts, but also highlighted the ethical imperative to distinguish validated alternatives from merely expedient ones ref [7]. More broadly, standards for hydrocephalus research have emphasized adverse-event reporting, transparent stopping rules, and patient-centered endpoints, because underpowered studies with optimistic mechanistic rationale can otherwise normalize prolonged exposure to ineffective therapies ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Critical Evaluation of Limitations, Controversies, and Methodological Challenges
subsections.subsection_title: Why many nonsurgical therapies have shown limited success
subsections.content:
Many nonsurgical therapies for hydrocephalus have shown limited success because they target downstream physiology rather than the dominant mechanical and developmental drivers of CSF circulation failure. Pharmacologic reduction of CSF production, for example with acetazolamide or furosemide, can transiently alter fluid dynamics but rarely reverses ventricular enlargement or the tissue-level consequences of impaired compliance and altered pulsatility; this mismatch was evident in clinical experience with posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation and other pediatric forms of hydrocephalus ref [54], ref [184]. Similar limitations apply to attempts to manipulate absorption or osmotic gradients without addressing obstruction, scarring, or evolving white-matter injury.

A second reason is that encouraging mechanistic signals in animal or short-term studies have translated poorly to clinically meaningful outcomes. In neonatal posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, interventions aimed at removing blood products or suppressing secondary injury have often reduced surrogate markers without reliably improving shunt dependence, neurodevelopment, or survival. The randomized DRIFT trial illustrated both the promise and difficulty of this approach, with delayed cognitive benefit emerging only in longer-term follow-up and substantial procedural complexity limiting generalizability ref [175], ref [185]. More broadly, the history of medical treatment has been marked by small, heterogeneous cohorts and inconsistent endpoints, making apparent benefits difficult to reproduce ref [84], ref [35].

Finally, hydrocephalus is not a single disease but a syndrome spanning congenital malformations, hemorrhagic injury, infection, tumor-related obstruction, and adult CSF disorders such as normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Therapies effective in one biological context may be irrelevant or unsafe in another. This etiologic heterogeneity, coupled with narrow therapeutic windows and concern for adverse effects in vulnerable infants, has constrained escalation from proof-of-concept to standard care ref [35], ref [186], ref [126]. Consequently, nonsurgical options have remained adjunctive or temporizing rather than definitive.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Research Priorities in Nonsurgical Hydrocephalus Therapy
subsections.content:
A central priority for nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy is to move beyond syndromic diagnosis toward biomarker-guided patient selection. Ventricular size alone poorly captures disease activity, treatment responsiveness, or mechanistic heterogeneity. In idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), MRI markers such as disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid-space hydrocephalus and related morphologic indices have improved phenotyping and may help enrich trials for patients most likely to benefit from targeted interventions rather than empirical management ref [187], ref [40]. Phase-contrast MRI studies of aqueductal CSF stroke volume also illustrate both the promise and the limitations of single-parameter selection tools, underscoring the need for multimodal biomarker panels ref [124].

CSF and blood biomarkers are especially attractive for distinguishing hydrocephalus subtypes from neurodegenerative mimics and for identifying biologically relevant endotypes. Work in iNPH has shown that amyloid-β and tau profiles can reveal overlapping Alzheimer pathology, which influences prognosis and may confound assessment of drug effects ref [188], ref [189]. More recent studies suggest that neurofilament light chain and other axonal injury markers correlate with disease severity and postoperative outcome, raising the possibility that they could serve as pharmacodynamic readouts in future medical trials ref [190]. Parallel advances in diffusion MRI and glymphatic-oriented imaging further suggest that periventricular white-matter injury and impaired fluid clearance may provide mechanistically informative stratification variables ref [191], ref [192].

Future biomarker programs should therefore emphasize integrated models combining imaging, CSF or plasma analytes, intracranial pressure or infusion testing, and standardized clinical phenotypes. International guideline efforts already stress that diagnosis and prognostication in iNPH require composite assessment rather than reliance on any single test ref [7]. For nonsurgical therapy development, the most useful biomarkers will be those that are reproducible across centers, sensitive to short-term biological change, and explicitly linked to a targetable pathway such as CSF secretion, neuroinflammation, fibrosis, or impaired clearance.

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Research Priorities in Nonsurgical Hydrocephalus Therapy
subsections.content:
Progress in nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy depends on models that capture the etiologic heterogeneity of the disorder rather than ventricular enlargement alone. Experimental systems have clarified that hydrocephalus can emerge from distinct but intersecting mechanisms, including impaired CSF absorption, developmental ciliary dysfunction, posthemorrhagic fibrosis and inflammation, and altered brain compliance. Kaolin and blood-injection models remain useful for testing pressure- and fibrosis-directed interventions, whereas genetic models have been particularly informative for defining ependymal and motile cilia biology relevant to congenital disease ref [193], ref [194], ref [3].

Mechanistic work increasingly links hydrocephalus to disruption of ventricular lining integrity and CSF-flow regulation. Studies in Ccdc39-deficient mice demonstrated that defective motile cilia can directly produce neonatal hydrocephalus ref [195], while ependymal denudation and altered subcommissural organ signaling have been implicated in aqueductal and communicating phenotypes ref [196], ref [197]. In parallel, intraventricular hemorrhage models show that iron toxicity, TGF-beta signaling, extracellular matrix deposition, and arachnoid scarring may sustain ventricular expansion after the acute event, highlighting tractable molecular targets for anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, or iron-chelating therapy ref [198], ref [12].

A priority for translation is to integrate these models with human data: patient-derived organoids, CSF and imaging biomarkers, and longitudinal phenotyping should be used to map mechanisms to treatable subtypes. Such alignment may also help explain why pharmacologic approaches have historically failed in unselected populations and support preclinical pipelines that use clinically relevant end points, including neurodevelopment, white-matter injury, and glymphatic or CSF-flow metrics rather than ventricular size alone ref [194], ref [3], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Research Priorities in Nonsurgical Hydrocephalus Therapy
subsections.content:
A central future direction is to move beyond single-agent paradigms toward rational combination and adjunctive strategies that target the multiple biological processes driving hydrocephalus progression, including CSF hypersecretion, inflammation, fibrosis, ependymal injury, and secondary white-matter damage. Experimental work suggests that combining etiology-directed therapy with CSF-modulating agents may be more effective than either approach alone. For example, the NKCC1 inhibitor bumetanide reduced CSF secretion in choroid plexus models, providing a mechanistic basis for pairing secretion-targeted drugs with anti-inflammatory or anti-fibrotic interventions in selected patients ref [199]. In posthemorrhagic settings, where iron toxicity and innate immune activation are prominent, combination regimens that integrate clot clearance, iron chelation, and inflammatory pathway suppression are particularly attractive ref [200], ref [201].

Adjunctive neuroprotection is another underdeveloped area. The failure of broad empiric medical therapy in historical hydrocephalus trials does not preclude benefit from biologically matched add-on treatments designed to preserve periventricular tissue while surgery addresses pressure and flow abnormalities. In neonatal and hemorrhagic models, anti-inflammatory approaches targeting TLR4-NF-kappaB signaling, transforming growth factor-beta–related fibrosis, or thrombin-mediated injury have each shown disease-modifying potential, implying that multi-target combinations could better limit ventricular expansion and downstream brain injury than monotherapy ref [202], ref [203], ref [204].

Clinically, adjunctive treatment strategies should also be evaluated around surgery rather than only as alternatives to it. Perioperative pharmacologic therapy might reduce shunt dependence in transient forms, improve endoscopic third ventriculostomy durability by limiting cisternal scarring, or mitigate long-term neurodevelopmental sequelae even when ventricular size is incompletely normalized. The acetazolamide–furosemide experience in posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation illustrates both the appeal and the limitations of nonspecific combinations, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided regimens, careful toxicity monitoring, and trials powered for functional outcomes rather than ventricular metrics alone ref [54], ref [205], ref [184].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Research Priorities in Nonsurgical Hydrocephalus Therapy
subsections.content:
Precision medicine in nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy will require moving beyond syndromic labels toward mechanism-defined subgroups. Etiologies such as posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, congenital ciliary disorders, aqueductal stenosis, idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus, and neuroinflammatory communicating hydrocephalus likely differ in CSF production, ependymal integrity, glymphatic transport, venous compliance, and inflammatory signaling, implying that a single pharmacologic strategy is unlikely to generalize across all patients. Genotype-first approaches are especially promising in congenital disease, where defects in motile cilia and ependymal development have been linked to hydrocephalus, including pathogenic variation in CCDC88C and MPDZ, thereby motivating subtype-specific targeting of ciliary, barrier, or junctional biology rather than empiric symptom control alone ref [206], ref [207].

Therapeutic stratification should also incorporate age and pathobiology. In preterm posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, intraventricular blood products, iron toxicity, and TGF-beta-driven fibrosis may identify infants most likely to benefit from anti-inflammatory, iron-chelating, or anti-scarring adjuncts, whereas secretory states marked by choroid plexus NKCC1-dependent transport may favor CSF-production–modulating therapies ref [208], ref [209]. In adult iNPH, biomarker-enriched selection may help distinguish patients dominated by CSF dynamic dysfunction from those with substantial concomitant Alzheimer pathology, a distinction supported by CSF biomarker studies and molecular imaging ref [210], ref [211]. Such enrichment could clarify when medical therapies should complement, defer, or be prioritized alongside shunting.

A practical precision-medicine framework would therefore combine deep phenotyping across imaging, CSF and blood biomarkers, genetics, and longitudinal treatment response. Large multicenter cohorts and molecularly annotated registries will be necessary to validate endotypes and support adaptive trials of subtype-matched interventions. Experience from recent genomic analyses of congenital hydrocephalus and transcriptomic studies implicating neurodevelopmental and inflammatory programs suggests that actionable subclasses are biologically plausible and clinically relevant ref [212], ref [213].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Research Priorities in Nonsurgical Hydrocephalus Therapy
subsections.content:
Clinical trials for nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy should move beyond conventional fixed two-arm designs because the disorder is heterogeneous, outcomes evolve over long follow-up periods, and event rates can be modest. Master protocols with shared infrastructure, adaptive randomization, and Bayesian borrowing can improve efficiency while preserving rigor, particularly when testing repurposed agents across mechanistically defined subgroups. The broader methodological rationale for adaptive and platform approaches is well established in contemporary trial science and is especially relevant where multiple candidate interventions and uncertain treatment-response modifiers coexist ref [214], ref [215].

Outcome selection also requires innovation. Reliance on shunt placement or radiographic ventricular size alone is insufficient, since clinically meaningful benefit may involve neurodevelopment, gait, cognition, intracranial pressure dynamics, and caregiver-reported function. Core outcome set methodology offers a route to harmonized endpoints, while enrichment strategies can incorporate imaging, CSF biomarkers, or physiology to identify patients most likely to respond and to support smaller, signal-detection studies ref [216], ref [217]. For hydrocephalus specifically, lessons from adult normal-pressure hydrocephalus trials underscore the value of prospectively standardized diagnostic criteria, multimodal baseline phenotyping, and blinded assessment of gait and cognitive outcomes ref [91], ref [218].

Pragmatic and registry-embedded randomized trials may be particularly powerful for rare hydrocephalus subtypes and for adjunctive therapies used alongside surgery, reducing cost and improving generalizability. Such trials should prespecify longitudinal estimands, missing-data handling, and Bayesian or group-sequential stopping rules, and they should incorporate decentralized follow-up where feasible. Existing guidance on pragmatic design and estimand frameworks can help align trial questions with real-world decision making and accelerate the evaluation of nonsurgical therapies in heterogeneous hydrocephalus populations ref [219], ref [220], ref [221].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Research Priorities in Nonsurgical Hydrocephalus Therapy
subsections.subsection_title: Health systems, access, and global relevance
subsections.content:
The future role of nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy will depend not only on biological efficacy but also on whether it can address inequities in diagnosis, referral, and longitudinal care. Hydrocephalus imposes a substantial global burden, particularly in low-resource settings where postinfectious disease remains common and access to neurosurgical services is limited; landmark epidemiologic and global surgery analyses underscore large unmet need in children and major workforce and infrastructure gaps for essential neurosurgical care ref [222], ref [223], ref [224]. In such contexts, scalable medical or adjunctive therapies could be especially valuable if they reduce time to treatment, stabilize patients before transfer, or lower the frequency of shunt dependence and revision.

Global relevance also requires therapies to be matched to heterogeneous disease ecologies. Studies from sub-Saharan Africa have shown that infant hydrocephalus is often linked to neonatal infection and distinct pathogen patterns, emphasizing that prevention, antimicrobial stewardship, and context-specific adjunctive therapies should be integrated rather than viewed separately from definitive CSF diversion ref [225], ref [226]. At the same time, long-term outcome studies highlight that hydrocephalus is a chronic condition requiring durable follow-up, developmental surveillance, and family support, making health-system integration central to any nonsurgical strategy ref [227], ref [228].

Accordingly, future trials should include implementation endpoints—feasibility, affordability, supply-chain robustness, and compatibility with task-shared care pathways—alongside conventional efficacy measures. International guidance on essential neurosurgical care and recent analyses of hydrocephalus service delivery suggest that progress will require hub-and-spoke referral networks, standardized follow-up protocols, and pragmatic interventions that remain effective where imaging, laboratory monitoring, and specialist access are constrained ref [223], ref [224], ref [229]. Ensuring global relevance therefore means designing nonsurgical therapies for real-world delivery across diverse health systems, not only for tertiary centers in high-income settings.
